common_name: Rusk Citrange (Historic Cold-Hardy Swingle-Bred Orange Hybrid)

planting.note: Plant grafted or container-grown trees in spring in well-drained soil in full sun; Rusk is one of botanist Walter Swingle's original 1890s citrange hybrids, chosen for fruit quality closer to sweet orange than most of its siblings.

directions: Rusk citrange dates to Walter Swingle's earliest USDA hybridization trials, crossing sweet orange with trifoliate orange in 1897 in response to the catastrophic Florida freezes of the 1890s, and was named for J.M. Rusk, the first U.S. Secretary of Agriculture. Compared with many other citranges bred in the same trials, Rusk fruit was noted for holding up better in fresh use, though it still carries more acid and seed than a true sweet orange and shines brightest in ade, marmalade, or juice. The tree takes on the trifoliate parent's light thorns and semi-deciduous winter habit, dropping some leaves in hard cold, and tolerates freezes well beyond what a standard orange survives once wood is mature. Give young trees a sheltered site and winter protection for their first two or three seasons in the Gulf South before letting them fend for themselves.

planting.note: Plant grafted or container-grown trees in spring in well-drained soil in full sun; Savage was singled out among Swingle's original citrange introductions for fruit that most closely approaches sweet orange in size and eating quality.

directions: Savage citrange came out of the same 1897 sweet orange x trifoliate orange hybridization work by USDA botanist Walter Swingle that produced Rusk, Morton, and the other early named citranges, all bred to push edible citrus north of where true oranges reliably survive. USDA citrus researcher Herbert Webber singled Savage out among that group as coming closest to a true sweet orange in size, color, and fresh-eating quality, though the fruit still carries more seeds and tartness than modern orange cultivars. Trees inherit trifoliate orange's cold hardiness and semi-deciduous habit along with modest thorns, tolerating hard freezes well past the point that would kill standard orange trees outright. Plant in full sun on well-drained soil and shelter young trees through their first couple of winters in the Gulf South before treating them as an established, self-sufficient planting.

planting.note: Plant grafted or container-grown trees in spring in well-drained soil in full sun; US-852 tolerates winter cold to around 0 degrees F once dormant, among the hardiest citrandarins available to home growers.

directions: US-852 was bred in 1965 by USDA researcher Joe Furr at the Indio, California field station, crossing Changsha mandarin with a large-flowered trifoliate orange selection to combine mandarin flavor with trifoliate orange's exceptional cold hardiness. Among the citrandarin group of USDA cold-hardy citrus hybrids, US-852 is regarded as one of the better-flavored for fresh eating, with a sweeter, less bitter profile than many trifoliate crosses, though fruit remains seedy and more tart than a standard mandarin. The tree shows the trifoliate parent's light thorns and part-deciduous winter habit and tolerates temperatures near 0 degrees F once wood is fully dormant and hardened off, well beyond what any true mandarin survives. Give it full sun and good drainage, and protect young trees through their first winters before relying on their cold tolerance in a Gulf Coast dooryard planting.

planting.note: Plant grafted or container-grown trees in spring in well-drained soil in full sun; Tavares is a sister introduction to Eustis limequat, crossed from oval Nagami-type kumquat rather than round kumquat, and is now much less commonly offered by nurseries.

directions: Tavares was released in 1913 alongside Eustis and Lakeland as part of Walter Swingle's original USDA limequat introductions, but unlike its round-kumquat-parented siblings, Tavares was crossed from Key lime and oval (Nagami-type) kumquat, giving it a somewhat different fruit shape and rind character. Like other limequats, the whole fruit is edible skin and all, with a tart, aromatic lime-flavored flesh inside a thin, kumquat-sweet rind, useful sliced fresh, juiced, or preserved. It shares the group's strong cold hardiness relative to true limes, tolerating freezes that would seriously damage or kill Key lime or Persian lime trees, though it remains less commonly propagated commercially today than Eustis. Grow it in full sun on well-drained soil, protect young trees through their first winters, and expect a compact, productive shrub-like tree well suited to large containers or small Gulf Coast garden beds.

planting.note: Plant grafted or container-grown trees in spring in well-drained soil in full sun; Lakeland is a sister seedling to Eustis limequat from the same 1909 Key lime x round kumquat cross, but has stayed a minor collector's variety rather than the commercial standard.

directions: Lakeland was released in 1913 as one of three original USDA limequats bred by Walter Swingle from a cross of Key lime and round (Meiwa/Marumi-type) kumquat, sharing its exact parentage with the far more widely planted Eustis limequat from the same breeding batch. Like Eustis, the small, gold-orange fruit combines a genuinely tart lime-flavored interior with an edible, mild, sweet kumquat rind, so the whole fruit can be eaten out of hand, sliced into drinks, or preserved. It carries the same strong cold tolerance that makes limequats useful where true limes cannot survive outdoors, but nurseries propagated Eustis far more heavily over the following century, leaving Lakeland a comparatively rare named selection today. Grow it exactly as you would Eustis, in full sun and well-drained soil, with winter protection while young and full sun exposure to maximize fruit sweetness.

planting.note: Plant container-grown rootstock liners in spring in well-drained soil in full sun, then graft a desired citrus scion onto the young rootstock; Troyer is grown as an understock, not for its own bitter, seedy fruit.

directions: Troyer citrange was produced in 1909 by USDA breeder E.M. Savage under Walter Swingle's direction at Riverside, California, crossing Washington Navel orange with trifoliate orange, and takes its name from the Alabama grower who received the first fruiting budwood. It became a cornerstone rootstock during California's mid-20th-century tristeza virus crisis, when UC Riverside's Bill Bitters screened hundreds of rootstock-scion combinations and found Troyer, along with its sister selection Carrizo from the same navel orange x trifoliate parentage, resistant to the disease that was devastating sour-orange-rooted groves. Troyer imparts strong cold tolerance, good tristeza resistance, and vigorous, well-anchored growth to whatever citrus variety is grafted onto it, though it is more sensitive than Carrizo to certain heavy or poorly drained soils. Home growers wanting a hardy, disease-resistant understock for grafting favorite citrus in a Gulf Coast dooryard planting can use Troyer much as they would Carrizo, providing full sun and good drainage for best results.
